📌If you are anxious around other people. Here are three things you need to know:-

1- Inward focus - This means you're totally focused on how you are perceived by other people - instead, make a more concious effort to shift your focus to one of outward curiosity, towards the other people -i.e  What do you want to know about other people in the room? 

2- Prone to the spotlight effect- you over estimate how much other's are judging you. Research shows we get this wrong most of the time. In reality, People are less concerned about us than we think. Reminding yourself of this enables you to recognize the bias and take back your power.

comment_text:
REMEMBER PEOPLE: before you start thinking or saying you have social anxiety (or any psychological disorder), consider the following:

1. Are your experiences different from the norm? Everyone experiences some stress at large or unfamiliar social situations. Do you experience it excessively or in inappropriate situations?

2. Does it cause extreme amounts of stress? Is the anxiety you feel overbearing, more than what it should be?

3. Does it significantly impact your ability to live? Again, everyone experiences stress with social situations. But most people are not strongly impaired by said stress. Do you struggle more than normal with life as a result?

If you experience these 3, THEN you can reasonably consider getting diagnosed by a professional. There is an extremely problematic epidemic of self diagnosis in the modern day, which is only getting worse due to the overgeneralization and desensitation to serious medical terms.

Thank you.

comment_text:
I had debilitating social anxiety until I was around 23 or 24 (I am now 39). I mostly hid it well - it usually externalized as appearing "shy", but internally, it was a war in my head. I had my close group of 5 friends that I was comfortable around, but pretty much anything outside of that was a struggle. Seemingly benign things like aunts and uncles visiting and asking me how school was would send my brain into an internal frenzy.

I know this won't help everyone, but I think sharing what helped me may be valuable. A couple years before my social anxiety was cured, I got really deep into meditation and mindfulness. I would meditate multiple times a week and eventually got to a point where I could get into mental states equivalent to an ego death psychedelic experience in a 30 minute meditation session. The one that would really do it for me is Sam Harris' "Waking Up" meditation exercise. I highly recommend giving it a shot and doing it regularly until you literally feel your whole body dissolve when you do it.

One day I decided to meditate on my social anxiety and reflect on why I had these feelings. I realized it's all in my head, it's ridiculous and makes no sense. I had a moment of true enlightenment, one of two in my life. I realized that I don't need to care about what people think. I am me, I am valuable, I have things to offer the world, and the worst thing that can happen if I put myself out there is that I'm not someone's cup of tea, and that's ok. Putting myself out there will connect me with the people that appreciate me for me, and I can surround myself with those people.

After that, I was a completely different person. It was still very nerve wracking at the beginning, but I would force myself to do things like pick the checkout in the grocery store with the cutest cashier, and after I paid for my groceries I would smile and give her a compliment before grabbing my groceries and heading out. As terrifying as it was at first, every time I did this they were flattered and I could tell it made their day. As I did this more and more, it reinforced that there was nothing to be scared of and the world doesn't need to be a scary place. I became a completely different confident man almost overnight.

For those that got this far: You are beautiful, you are unique, you are a gift to the universe, and you are loved. Embrace yourself, believe in yourself. You deserve it. I wish you all the best <3

In part i think it has to do with my own beliefs about myself but also the nature of modern social dynamics. comment_text: i think what scared me most about burnout was how slowly it happened. there wasn't one day where i suddenly felt completely broken. i just gradually stopped looking forward to things, started waking up tired, became more impatient with people and needed more and more time alone just to feel normal again. because it happened so gradually, i kept thinking it was just a busy period and that i'd feel better once things calmed down. i eventually realized i had been saying “once things calm down” for months. that's when i started looking into the whole reset idea and came across Reset Your Body and Mind by Morgan Lane. what stuck with me was the idea of rebuilding your basics before trying to become more productive. fixing sleep, getting some movement in, spending less time consuming random stuff and actually leaving some space in the day to do nothing. it wasn't some dramatic overnight change, but after a few weeks i realized i wasn't constantly waiting for the day to be over anymore. that was probably the first sign that something was actually changing.

.

I have Chronic Fatique Syndrome. And exhaustion, two fold because i have the exhaustion what comes with CFS and exhaustion by itself (at least that is how it feels like). I have also have insomnia and depression, so it all adds up. Anyway, in order to get myself to wake up in the morning for work or an appt, I use visualization. In my case it is something I came up with on my own a couple of years ago.
Because I hate morning I try to make it as efficient as possible. This includes choosing my waredrobe the night before. On the floor, on the side of my bed, I have (in a row), my purse, work bag, shoes, and clothes lidded bucket (to keep my clothes nearby but mostly cat hair free). When I wake up, I will sit up, put all of my stuff on the bed around me and check my e-mail (or do app check ins) while I get ready. On the other side of my bed is my jewelry box and a bag of my medications. So, I have done every single thing I need to do before I have gotten out of bed, including gotten dressed.
The point of this is that when the alarm first goes off, I give myself two minutes two wake up, in that time I will work through a visual step by step plan of getting ready, including things that aren't normal for that morning's routine. I think it is because my Asperger's Syndrome now knows what is going to happen and agrees to do it in that order (fewer surprises and anxieties). It's my way of talking myself into getting up and leaving! It helps. I call out or call in late less often than I did. "Sense of familiarity" ... Sure, that works. I had not thought of it in that way before.

comment_text: I experienced this when I ended up homeless for about three months. Before that happened, the thought of living on the streets terrified me. Both homeless and homed people who I interacted with were overwhelmingly decent. Some wanted to know if I needed anything and some just were bored and wanted company. And I realized that I could read people and dodge sketchy situations very well. Which is a skill I didn't know I had until it was tested and I ended up more confident and less afraid, and more happy than I'd been in in years, because I had a regular route and chatted up with some familiar, safe people when I was on it. Before that, I'd been stuck at home in a neighborhood where everyone drove and no one walked, where people stayed inside doing their own things and neighbors didn't talk and my most reliable social outlet was online gaming so I'd play games even though I'd rather just have somewhere to meet people locally that's more easy than it really is. This all really makes me think its cars and devices and all the technologies we depend on that are making us all more isolated.

comment_text:
Here are some signs from experience:
1.They make you feel like something they did was your fault. Also, I’ve had people do this and say “it’s just a joke” big red flag. It gets to a point where it stops being funny and starts to hurt.
2. When you ask them to hang out, they say they are busy and then send you pictures of them hanging out on that day with all your other friends. This one hurts so bad. You have to remember that it’s not a problem for them to have other friends, that is something you always have to remember, but you also have to be aware of when your friends are trying to make you left out. It’s good for them to have other friends, but they shouldn’t make you feel left out for it.
3. They don’t listen when you tell them to stop. Whether it’s an insensitive joke or a basic request, a real friend doesn’t push past a boundary a friend sets, which brings me to my next point
4. They make you feel scared to set boundaries and when you set them, they make you feel bad. For example: you tell your friends to please stop making comments about your looks and instead of listening, they tell you that it’s “just a joke” and that you have “no sense of humor” or they say that they “didn’t mean it that way”. If they do this, no matter how small the boundary may be, they are not a true friend. 
5. (Ok, this one is kinda specific but that’s because it has REALLY bothered me) when they say you are “such an only child and are bad at sharing” when you do everything for them and they won’t give you the most basic things. I have been called an “only child” in a derogatory way all because I didn’t want to give them my whole lunch because they “didn’t want to pack a lunch that day” but the second I asked if I could hold their squishy, they acted like I asked them to give me 1000 dollars and got mad at me. I had people who would grab my things that I had asked them not to touch, but the second I don’t give them something, I am “bad at sharing” and again, these people wouldn’t let me borrow their sharpie for 2 minutes. This one is wrong in many ways: they are a hypocrite, they don’t respect your boundaries, they shame and embarrass you (because often they would say this in front of a bunch of people to embarrass me), and they don’t want to put effort into you.
6. They don’t appologize, they just ignore the issue and pretend it never happens. Real friends take accountability for their actions.
7. They don’t let you talk. If you want to talk about anything, they interrupt you and don’t ever let you finish. It’s one thing to interrupt, we all do that sometimes, but when they change the subject after they are done and don’t let you finish what you had to say, red flag.
8. This is the final one, you only stay with them because you don’t know what to do without them/you have been friends for such a long time, it doesn’t feel right to leave.
Anyways, hope this helps 🫶

I dunno whether or not I'm outgrowing my friendships or not but lately I just feel very spiteful. Most of my IRL friendships died some time before covid, I was in a very busy place in my life and by the time I got around to making new friends through work, that's when covid happened. Some of them left our office for different jobs and I was left alone again. After that time, my only friends were online connections that I had for years. 
Over time, I started noticing that our differences weren't be tollerated and overcome but continued to persist and fester into arguments and I realized the real limits of online only friendships. 

I noticed that the kinds of arguments that we would have were very juvenile in nature and I found myself arguing and saying things that I would have never said to any of my friends 10 years prior. That's when it dawned on me that with those people it just felt like there were a lot of 'stuck' people and they were really just holding me back. 
They had serious arrested development and I could see it in the frustrations that would boil over between other people on the server.

Its one thing to have problems, long term problems even. But its another thing entirely to have the same gripes and issues and way of talking with people so many years after you've first met. 
Bottom line is you need to keep trying to find your people because you're going to realize when you do that, you find people who are actually mature enough to spend time with and you'll be pleasantly surprised that that also would like to spend time with you. 
Raise your standards. And maybe just maybe, some of the friends you had before will come along too.

Friendship can increase the level of our performance, help us go through the problems, and improve our health.                              These bonds in childhood and early years can shape our emotional growth, beliefs and values.

Making and maintaining friends can be uneasy.

Scientists defined this as the "liking gap", which means that others usually like and rate us better than we do. Companionships are the bonds people form based on common interests, hobbies, or values. Sometimes, it is just participation in the same class or team. Its results are an increase os self-esteem and our resilience to stress.
On the other hand, closeness is a friendship with a more developed level of intimacy, built on sharing thoughts and feelings            as well as supporting each other. comment_text:
For about a year now, my friendship with my closest friend has been increasingly destroying me, and the worst part is that I'm unable to say anything. 
It happened three times. 
These three conversations hurt me deeply because I felt like what she was saying confirmed and reinforced everything my "dark voice" was telling me. 

What I call my dark voice is all the thoughts, doubts, and shame I repeat to myself internally out of pure insecurity and lack of confidence in what I'm thinking or doing. 
And while I needed a more measured and calm perspective, my friend is the "direct" type : 
When we laugh together or talk about our lives, it's fine, but when I already doubt what I'm doing and her reaction confirms what I already think about myself in a negative way, it hurts terribly. 
It's like I'm in a guillotine, and without realizing it, her contradictory reaction, or when she implies I've messed up with a sigh or a tone of voice, cuts the rope holding the blade. 

It hasn't just destroyed my morale, but also the trust I have in her. 
Before, I'd show her almost every time I finished a drawing, but now I panic at the thought of asking her opinion. 
The moment I realized something had broken was when I thought I'd messed up : I'd made a homepage to promote my commissions, but since I'd copied the structure of another creator's artwork, just with a few different elements, I was afraid I'd copied instead of being inspired. 

I wanted to ask her opinion, and as soon as I remembered the last time I'd asked her for feedback on my video, I immediately got scared. 
I handle criticism very poorly, so I decided to keep quiet if I wanted to avoid crying again. 

After several days of feeling guilty about this potential unintentional plagiarism, I went to ask for help from another friend I had known for less than a year, and after a few ideas she gave me, I felt better and started working on it again.

I know I could just tell her, but mentally I'm simply incapable of it. 

Even though she's someone very important to me, I don't think I can recover from what her words did to me. 
I think the solution is simply to move on. 
Remembering those three conversations brings back all my insecurities, my shame, my fears, my doubts, my failures, and all of it means I can no longer look at what I used to create or do without feeling visceral shame. 

With my current friends ( many of whom I only speak English with ), I feel like I'm just a cringe-loving kid who thinks that being cringe is ultimately about being free. 
Most of them are young artists, aged 11 to 19 ( I'm 17 ), and since our conversations remain superficial and purely artistic, they do me good. 
I'd like to be able to trust the friend I asked for advice on my artwork a bit more, as I was completely lost, and so far I think it's going well. 
I still find it hard to take the initiative and write to her about personal matters, but that will come with time. 

Regarding my friend whom I've known for several years and whose words hurt me, I don't know where things will go.
I love this friend, really, but our friendship has hurt me, and if I want to move on, I'd better distance myself.

I tell myself that I am not leaving this friend but that I am distancing myself from the relationship we have so that I don't have to think about it anymore.

I call it the "spare tire". My brother actually came up with that term when we were kids in a not-so-nice instance in which he had a friend he referred to in that way. I have usually made friends through various groups and activities in which I had a leadership role. I think part of the problem in my situation is when they got to know me beyond that and lo and behold found out I had needs too and did not have all the answers then they lost interest or viewed it as a burden. This is part of why I no longer take on leadership roles in groups, and in the one activity where I do (breeding rats) I don't let relationships get to a friendship level anymore. I keep it strictly business.  Also find that when those interests go away in one form or another so do the friends you make in those settings. When the one friend I made who got rats from me lost them of old age she no longer wanted to be friends and get together anymore even though we still both had other animals that we shared an interest in.

There's another dynamic I have found that women who are married often make friends when they are on the outs with their husband and they really love all the support you give them through those hard times and then when they start getting along with their husband better they stop sharing and drop the closeness as if to say "OK, enough of this. In America, sadly, people are socialized to equate one's value (and the value of others) with what they produce. I've always found this abhorrent, but it is deeply baked into our society. This is why so often seniors are treated as useless and people no longer make time for them, and why being unemployed is regarded with such judgement. 

Tangibles like money and material things seem to be given a higher value than intangibles, so if you're poor and can't afford to take your friend out to lunch and they are of a higher income bracket, that can be a problem even though those circumstances are beyond your control and you may give in less measurable or less material ways. They will never view it as equal. 

We live in a consumerist, capitalist society and I really believe that has a big impact on human relationships. This is not a simple mess to sort out. I think core values need to change to become a more humanistic society in which people don't feel the need to "earn" love, kindness, and to be valued by those around them, and the example needs to start at the top. Dogs prioritize what they see as high value treats and behave accordingly. Humans should be more evolved than that.

The "old friendship" mostly happens on the phone, you only see each other every few months or even less. And If you doo meet, it is usually coffee or eating, so basically talking, again. These friendships are not nurtured by new shared experiences, they are basically nostalgia. And they are usually stuck in the mindset when the shared experience actually happened - a long time ago. comment_text: Self doubt lives in the body, not just the mind. When your nervous system is chronically activated (shallow breathing, tight chest, elevated heart rate), your brain interprets that as danger and defaults to avoidance and second guessing. You cannot think your way out of a state your body is creating. The most effective way I have found to break self doubt is to voluntarily put yourself in situations where your body screams at you to quit and you choose to stay. Cold water immersion does this better than anything. When you sit in an ice bath and your entire nervous system is firing, telling you to get out, and you breathe through it and stay calm, you build a reference point. Your body learns that discomfort does not equal danger. That reference point transfers to everything. Public speaking, hard conversations, business decisions. I facilitate breathwork and cold exposure sessions and the people who arrive full of self doubt are often the ones who leave with the most clarity. Not because I gave them a pep talk. Because they proved something to themselves with their own body. Confidence built through experience is the only kind that lasts.

Note to self =

Procrastination is a protective mechanism:

A primitive part of the brain, known as the "Amygdala" involved with fight, flight, or freeze chooses flight and results in you turning a less stressful activity. Accompanied by poor emotional regulation, low self esteem, and high standards result in procrastination, not necessarily laziness. Discipline and strict time management can make it worse as you feel more stressed, looping back to procrastination.

What to do?
1.) Regulate emotions by addressing/acknowledging them through journaling, or talking to someone about it. This can help reduce negative emotion.
2.) Remove nearby distractions like keeping your phone in a separate room, uninstalling addictive apps, putting blockers, or putting it in a different log in of your computer.
3.) You may spiral into rumination if you don't also develop and cultivate an attitude of self-compassionate where you forgive yourself and make a plan to do better next time when you find yourself procrastinating.

My life has been all over the place these past few years.
I studied in the same school for 12 years, from kindergarten till class 10. I was always that kid who did well in studies (except maths... I've hated maths since forever 😭). I had amazing friends, life felt simple, and I genuinely believed I could do something.
Then everything changed.
I changed my school, took PCMB, started preparing for NEET and CET, and somewhere along the way I lost myself. I don't have any friends now. 
I messed up my 10th boards and scored only 65%. I know people say "10th marks don't matter," but for me they did. That was the first time my family completely lost faith in me. Ever since then, every mistake feels like proof that they're right.
My parents are spending almost ₹4 lakhs on my 11th and 12th coaching because they truly believe I'll become a doctor. Every morning I leave home at 7 and come back around 7 in the evening. It's exhausting.

If I ever come back here after wasting another day, I want this to remind me that no timetable, no motivational video, and no "perfect Monday" is going to change my life. Only sitting down and studying will.
Maybe I won't crack NEET. Maybe I will. I honestly don't know.
But I don't want to fail because I never tried.
If you're reading this, please keep me in your prayers. I hope one day I come back to this comment and smile because everything somehow worked out.

3. Memory Deficits (particularly Working and Short-Term Memory)
Common complaints include forgetting recent conversations, misplacing items, or forgetting why they entered a room or what they were about to say. This side effect predominantly affects short-term memory and working memory (the memory used for simultaneous task management). Long-term memory typically remains largely unaffected.

4. Verbal Slowing and Word-Finding Difficulty
Frequent "tip-of-the-tongue" phenomena—where the desired word feels accessible but cannot be verbally retrieved—along with prolonged pauses and hesitations during speech.

5. Emotional Blunting
This is a highly significant and sometimes more distressing side effect than the depression itself. The individual feels neither sad nor happy; their entire affective spectrum becomes flattened. This directly impacts social cognition and decision-making: they may no longer derive pleasure from achievements, become indifferent to unfolding events, and lack motivation for planning and goal-directed activities. Empathy and emotional connection with others may also be reduced.

6. Apathy and Lack of Motivation
This can be mistaken for depression, but it lacks the components of sadness and hopelessness. Rather, there is simply a complete absence of desire to engage in any activity. The individual prefers to sit passively and indifferently, which directly impairs executive function (planning, task initiation, and task completion).

7. Daytime Somnolence
Even with adequate sleep the night before, persistent drowsiness during the day can occur, which naturally severely compromises both concentration and memory.

8. Paradoxical Effect: Restlessness and Hyperarousal (in some individuals)
Because sertraline has a mild dopaminergic activating effect compared to some other SSRIs, a small subset of patients may experience inner restlessness (akathisia), mental agitation, pressured (rapid) speech, and racing thoughts. This state similarly makes sustained focus virtually impossible.

This video is excellent. Since I am not a native English speaker, I found the diction in this video quite overwhelming. I've included what I infer from this video below.
1 . Procrastination is not the cause. It is a symptom. It means procrastination appears since it is caused by something. Now, what is the cause?
2. The cause is that we feel we won't gain anything if we do the deed right now. I presume we now label the deed as "unattractive" since it won't give us any reward or thrill. Hence, we procrastinate. Now, why do we feel this way?
3. We feel this way due to the effect called "Temporal Proximity." What is it? It means the longer we know the reward will be obtained from doing the deed, the less we feel the reward's preciousness. It is also the same with the deadline. If the deadline is so far away, we see it as "achievable, and the urgency to meet it is not that high" rather than knowing it is so close to our current time. 

Now, this is the key. Temporal proximity has an impact on how we feel about the reward. The farther it is, the less precious it is. WE CAN TWEAK IT. 

But how?

First, we made the reward feel so close. Pomodoro Technique is an example. After doing considerable work and reaching specific milestones, we shall reward ourselves with an "Award." This could help us associate the deed with an "attractive deed."

Next, we imposed a specific deadline for each activity or milestone. This means we impose fear on ourselves. This works best if the fear comes from the outside party. Not from the inside. Not imposed by us, but imposed by authority or scary figures outside us.

comment_text:
I don't think people really understand exam pressure until they go through it. It sounds like someone wailing about some useless nonsense, until you realise it's an actual, real thing. And people react to it in different ways. I used to be the 'give up and stare at the clock' person, like literally. But now? Now, when I start to get consumed by doubts and negative thoughts like, 'you're gonna fail your GCSEs', 'you're cooked ', 'this question is a 5 marker... you can't do this,' 'I'm doomed', 'I didn't revise properly', 'why are there so many 5 markers?!!', 'I need to read the question for the 4th time', 'I'm losing time', 'I have 5 minutes',' I didn't re-check my answers', 'the answers not C, it's A', 'change it to A', 'what if it's C?', 'I'll lose a mark because I'm stupid'.........

I just stop. I stop writing, I stop thinking, I close the paper. And I just sit there for a good 5 minutes, and breathe. Deep breaths. 

And it actually works. 

It clears me out and I suddenly realise, it's not the end of the world. I don't need Grade 9s and 8s, that's what I would LIKE, but not what I need. I need a good Grade 5, and even a grade 4, it's a pass, isn't it? If you're not good at a subject, and you know you're not good at it, don't beg for a grade 9; just work hard for a pass. That's it, and that's a lot. People need to understand that getting a Grade 9 for every single subject is extremely unrealistic. If you get grade 7 and 6s, be proud, because that's hard to get. And just work hard, so you don't think back and wish you'd tried harder, cause I'm telling you, the only reason people fail, is because they give up.

'Believe in yourself, and you're already halfway there'


If you have exams, good luck, YOU'LL DO WELL 🎉🎉🎉🎉
